blurb: Sleek, smooth-coated German ratter, the short-haired counterpart of the Schnauzer
description: The German Pinscher is a medium-sized, endangered German breed with a short, smooth black-and-tan or red coat, once kept as a stable dog and ratter.
answer: The German Pinscher, or Deutscher Pinscher, is a medium-sized German breed in the Pinscher and Schnauzer group, essentially a short-haired counterpart of the Schnauzer. It stands about 45 to 50 cm tall, weighs 14 to 20 kg, and is now considered an endangered breed in Germany.

body: The breed's origins are unknown. Rough- and smooth-haired pinschers were traditionally kept as carriage and stable dogs and valued as ratters, and both types could appear in the same litter; the rough-haired type became the Standard Schnauzer. The smooth Pinscher is mentioned in 1836, was recorded in the German studbook in 1880, and the Pinscher-Schnauzer-Klub was founded in 1895.

After World War II the breed almost disappeared. Werner Jung rebuilt it from one standard-sized dog and four unusually large Miniature Pinschers, and a litter was whelped in 1958. The FCI accepted the breed in 1955. It remains listed as endangered by the German society for the conservation of old and endangered domestic breeds.

The German Pinscher is of medium size, with both sexes in the same height and weight range. The coat is dense, short and smooth, in black-and-tan or self-coloured red ranging from light stag-red to dark reddish brown. It is a distinct breed from the Affenpinscher, the Austrian Pinscher and the Miniature Pinscher.

Yes. It is listed as endangered in Germany; between 2008 and 2017 roughly 350 to 450 puppies were whelped each year.

faq.q: Is the German Pinscher recognised by the FCI?
faq.a: Yes. The FCI accepted it in 1955 and lists it as breed number 184 in Group 2, with Germany as the country of origin.
